newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade police back down in student standoff.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade police back down in student standoff.

text.p: Serbian opposition supporters streamed onto the streets of Belgrade early on Friday after police backed down from a 12-hour standoff with students and dismantled a cordon preventing them from marching.
More than 2,000 student protesters who had staged an evening street party in front of the police cordon were joined by thousands of jubilant Belgrade residents on foot and in cars.

The few security forces left on the streets dissuaded them from heading for the residential area where President Slobodan Milosevic lives. The protesters also abandoned plans to march to the Serbian government building to demand an order withdrawing police from the streets.
The crowd headed along main boulevards, enjoying their new-found freedom.
Armed riot police have been enforcing a ban on protest marches imposed after clashes between pro-government and opposition demonstrators on December 24.

The crowd planned to march past state television, which has virtually ignored the nearly eight weeks of protests. Every evening, protesters bang pots and pans and blow whistles, symbolically drowning out the sound of the main news broadcast.

One elderly woman came out onto her balcony in pyjamas blowing a whistle to greet the students, who had spent the evening dancing in front of the police cordon to music played on the demonstrators' public address system.
Witnesses said several people were injured when a car ploughed into the column of demonstrators but it was not clear how it happened.

Students set up their evening street party after an afternoon playing cat and mouse with police. As soon as one cordon broke up, students would start moving but a fresh police blockade would spring up somewhere else.
Thursday marked the 53rd consecutive day of protests against the cancellation of municipal election results by President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialists last November.
On Wednesday, Milosevic conceded that the opposition Zajedno coalition had won in Serbia's second city Nis, but Zajedno leaders vowed protests would continue until all their claims were met.
The United States said on Thursday Milosevic's concession did not go far enough and he could not win world applause by "dribbling out minor concessions".
"The Serbian government does not have the right to grant the opposition victories that the opposition won on its own in elections," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.
On Thursday, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum headed for The Hague, Brussels, Sarajevo and Zagreb to discuss the crisis in Serbia, deliberately excluding Belgrade.

After a regular meeting in the Dutch capital of U.S. and European Union foreign ministry officials, he will take part in a meeting in Brussels of the five-nation Contact Group on former Yugoslavia, made up of the United States, Britain, France, Germany and Russia.

France said it was sending Paul Poulade, director for continental Europe at the Foreign Ministry, to Belgrade to urge Milosevic to heed an Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) mission's confirmation of the opposition wins.
The government responded to the OSCE report by admitting Zajedno had won in nine wards of Belgrade and three smaller provincial cities.
But it said nothing about Belgrade's policy-making municipal assembly and contended that in the other cities no party won a majority or the results were inconclusive and required further examination.
